newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Larger NATO must keep north-south balance - Romania.
newsitem.headline: Larger NATO must keep north-south balance - Romania.

text.p: Romania's defence minister said on Friday that NATO's planned expansion into former communist countries in Eastern Europe should not upset the balance between the alliance's northern and southern flanks.

"Romania believes NATO's expansion must take place simultaneously on both flanks as expansion only to the north would create an imbalance," Victor Babiuc told reporters after returning from a tour of Germany, Norway and Holland.
"If we want a coherent expansion, then the balance between the two flanks from the military point of view must be considered very seriously."
Romania has won public support for its remote bid to win early admission to NATO from southern members France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Turkey and from Canada.

But Britain, the United States and Germany have given no explicit support. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic remain favourites to be named first candidates for membership at a NATO summit in Madrid in July.

Babiuc said none of NATO's 16 members opposed Romania's membership at some point and its chances of joining in the "first wave" were still under discussion, with growing sympathy from northern members.

He urged NATO states to consider Romania's position on the border of the "zone of risk," saying the country was "the only link missing in the southern flank and must be therefore considered for the first wave of expansion."
Romanian membership, he said, would help to persuade Russia that it had nothing to fear from NATO expansion after Moscow's conclusion this week of an accord with the alliance.

"The southern flank is more vulnerable because it is close to a zone of risk -- the Balkans, the Middle East where Islamic fundamentalism is operating, where there is drugs and arms trafficking and terrorism," Babiuc said.

Western governments have praised Romania's tough reforms and the signature of a post-communist treaty with Hungary and they have welcomed the prospect of a similar pact being concluded next month with ex-Soviet Ukraine.
Babiuc put the estimated cost of joining NATO at $3 billion and said Romania would incur far greater expense if it was left outside the alliance.
